title: The Effect of Crowding on Human Task Performance
research_question: What effect does population density per se have on human task performance (simple and complex tasks), and what role do temporal factors play in this effect?

participants.description: Experiment I: 126 high school students (84 boys, 42 girls) from Palo Alto, California, divided into 18 groups (12 male, 6 female), half with 5 subjects, half with 9 subjects. Experiment II: 306 high school students, divided into 34 groups of 7 to 9 each (18 male, 16 female). Experiment III: 180 women between the ages of 25 and 60, recruited through a temporary employment agency, run in groups of nine.
participants.recruitment: Experiment I: Newspaper ad offering $1.75/hour for 10 hours. Experiment III: Temporary employment agency.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Rooms of varying sizes: 160 sq ft (large), 80 sq ft (medium, Exp I only), and 35 sq ft (small). Subjects were seated on comfortable wooden chairs with desk-type arms. Rooms were equipped with air conditioning, rugs, sound insulation, water cooler, microphones, and speakers to control for physical discomfort, noise, temperature, and odors. Density was varied by placing 5 or 9 subjects in these rooms.

measures.instrument: Proposed solutions and best ideas identified by group
Number of specified numbers crossed out on a sheet of random numbers
Number of English words formed from given letters
Number of unique uses suggested for a common object (Object Uses task)
Number of common words recalled from a list
Number of English words solved from sets of five letters
Questionnaire covering biographical information and reactions

findings.quote: no main effects nor were there any interactions between density and any temporal measures that we looked at.

mechanisms: The initial hypothesis was that high population density acts as an aversive stimulus, raising drive level and affecting performance (facilitating simple tasks, interfering with complex tasks). However, the null findings suggest that density per se, under the controlled conditions of the experiments, does not function as an ordinary aversive, arousal-inducing stimulus.
The authors speculate that any effects of high density might be more complicated, primarily affecting social behaviors and interactions among people, rather than individual task performance.
moderators: Temporal factors (first vs. second task presentation, performance across days, duration of exposure)
implementation_implications: Density per se should not be considered inherently evil; if logistical problems (e.g., lack of air, noise, physical discomfort) can be solved, high density might not have negative effects on people and could even be encouraged or allowed in certain contexts.
The research suggests that concerns about urban concentrations and their negative effects should focus on logistical and organizational problems rather than density itself as an inherent social evil.

limitations: The possibility that the experimental design, tasks, measures, or subject population were inadequate to detect an effect.
The limited duration of crowding (4 hours) and subjects' awareness that it was temporary; effects might appear only with greater duration or if subjects are unaware of eventual relief.

The formal and structured nature of the experimental situation (individual chairs, specific tasks, limited verbal interaction, strangers, no long-term relationship, minimal physical movement) might have prevented density effects from emerging. The findings are limited to these specific conditions.
